questions.stem: An 82 year old woman has a 3 month history of breathlessness, tiredness and swollen ankles. She has gained 4 kg and now sleeps propped up on pillows. She had a myocardial infarction 6 years ago. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm, BP 136/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. She has pitting oedema to the shins and fine bibasal crackles.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Previous MI plus breathlessness, orthopnoea, weight gain and pitting oedema is fluid congestion from a failing pump: chronic heart failure.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Orthopnoea, weight gain and oedema = **fluid congestion**. A previous MI is a key cause.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A heart that cannot pump enough blood, causing congestion: **chronic heart failure**.

elim: No smoking history or wheeze, and COPD does not explain orthopnoea, weight gain and pitting oedema.
Can cause tiredness and weight gain but not orthopnoea, crackles and pitting oedema.
Gives fine crackles but not orthopnoea, weight gain or pitting oedema.
Causes oedema, but orthopnoea and a previous MI point to the heart, not the kidney.

steps.x: **A. Chronic heart failure.** Breathless + orthopnoea + oedema + weight gain after an MI = heart failure.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has 4 months of breathlessness on exertion and ankle swelling. He has type 2 diabetes, smokes 20 cigarettes a day and has had angina for 5 years. His NT-proBNP is raised. Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 34% with a hypokinetic anterior wall.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his heart failure?
questions.e: Coronary artery disease is the commonest cause of heart failure; angina, diabetes, smoking and a regional wall motion defect point to ischaemic HFrEF.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Angina + diabetes + smoking, and a **regional** (anterior) wall defect with EF 34% = ischaemic HFrEF.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The commonest cause of HF, and the one his risk factors predict: **coronary artery disease**.

elim: No alcohol history; dilated cardiomyopathy gives global, not regional, hypokinesia.
Causes thick, stiff walls with preserved EF rather than a regional wall motion defect.
Causes high-output failure with a preserved EF and a normal echo.
Follows a viral illness in a younger patient; he has angina and vascular risk factors.

steps.x: **C. Coronary artery disease.** Commonest cause of heart failure = coronary artery disease; a regional wall defect says ischaemia.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has 6 weeks of breathlessness on exertion. He now needs four pillows to sleep and wakes most nights coughing and breathless. He had an inferior myocardial infarction last year. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on auscultation of his chest?
o: Bronchial breathing at the right base
Fine inspiratory crackles at both bases
questions.e: Left ventricular failure raises pulmonary venous pressure, so fluid enters the alveoli and gives fine bibasal inspiratory crackles. Consolidation would give bronchial breathing with fever.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: wakes most nights coughing and breathless
steps.x: Orthopnoea + PND after an MI = **left-sided heart failure** with pulmonary congestion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fluid in the alveoli at both lung bases: **fine bibasal crackles**.

elim: Suggests consolidation; he has no fever or productive cough.
Suggests pleurisy or pulmonary infarction, not congestion.
A sign of life-threatening asthma, not heart failure.
Suggests a pneumothorax or large effusion on one side.

steps.x: **B. Fine inspiratory crackles at both bases.** Left heart failure = pulmonary congestion = bibasal crackles.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with severe pulmonary arterial hypertension has 2 months of increasing ankle swelling and an aching discomfort under her right ribs. She is not breathless lying flat. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm, BP 118/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Her chest is clear. She has pitting oedema to the knees and a smooth, tender liver edge.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?
questions.e: Pulmonary hypertension strains the right ventricle; right-sided failure causes systemic venous congestion: a raised JVP, hepatomegaly and peripheral oedema, with clear lungs.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Clear chest but oedema and a tender liver = **right-sided (congestive) heart failure**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Systemic venous congestion is seen in the neck: a **raised JVP**.

elim: A sign of aortic regurgitation.
A sign of left-sided failure with alveolar oedema; her chest is clear.
A sign of cardiac tamponade or severe asthma.
A sign of chronic liver disease, not congestive hepatomegaly.

steps.x: **D. Raised jugular venous pressure.** Right heart failure = peripheral oedema + hepatomegaly + raised JVP.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man has severe ischaemic heart failure with an ejection fraction of 18%. He is breathless at rest. On examination his radial pulse is regular, but every other beat is noticeably weaker than the one before. His BP is 96/64 mmHg and there are bibasal crackles.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for this pulse finding?
questions.e: Pulsus alternans (alternating strong and weak beats in a regular rhythm) reflects severe LV impairment and is a poor prognostic sign. Tamponade gives pulsus paradoxus instead.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: every other beat is noticeably weaker
steps.x: Regular rhythm, alternating strong and weak beats = **pulsus alternans**, with EF 18%.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pulsus alternans means a badly failing LV: **severe LV systolic impairment**.

elim: Gives a collapsing (water-hammer) pulse, not alternating strength.
Gives an irregularly irregular pulse; his rhythm is regular.
Gives pulsus paradoxus: the pulse weakens on inspiration.
Gives a jerky or bisferiens pulse.

steps.x: **E. Severe left ventricular systolic impairment.** Pulsus alternans = severe LV impairment = poor prognosis.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man with long-standing COPD (FEV1 32% predicted) has 2 months of worsening ankle swelling. He has smoked for 50 years. His pulse rate is 94 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 88% breathing air. He has a raised JVP, a loud P2, an enlarged liver and pitting oedema to mid-calf.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his ankle swelling?
questions.e: Long-standing COPD with chronic hypoxia causes pulmonary hypertension (loud P2) and then right ventricular failure: raised JVP, hepatomegaly and peripheral oedema.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Hypoxic COPD + loud P2 + raised JVP + big liver = **RV failure** (cor pulmonale).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Long-standing COPD complicated by **right ventricular failure**.

elim: He is not taking it, and it would not raise the JVP or enlarge the liver.
DVT is usually unilateral and does not raise the JVP or cause hepatomegaly.
Causes ankle oedema but not a raised JVP or hepatomegaly.
Low albumin oedema does not raise the JVP.

steps.x: **E. Right ventricular failure.** Long-standing COPD can complicate into RV failure: look for raised JVP, hepatomegaly, oedema.

questions.stem: An 80 year old man has 3 months of exertional breathlessness and two episodes of chest tightness while walking uphill. He now needs three pillows at night. His pulse is slow-rising and his BP is 112/90 mmHg. There is a harsh ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge radiating to the carotids, and fine bibasal crackles.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his heart failure?
questions.e: A slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure and an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids is aortic stenosis, a recognised cause of left ventricular failure.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure, ESM to the carotids = **aortic stenosis**, now with LVF.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Left ventricular failure caused by **aortic stenosis**.

elim: Gives right-sided signs with a raised JVP and no murmur.
Gives a mid-diastolic murmur at the apex, often with AF.
Causes right-sided failure with a loud P2, not an ejection murmur to the carotids.
Gives a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge with giant v waves.

steps.x: **A. Aortic stenosis.** Causes of LVF: ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has had left ventricular failure for 6 years after an anterior myocardial infarction. Over the last 2 months his legs have swollen to the thighs and his abdomen feels full. His pulse rate is 90 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. His JVP is raised to the earlobes and his liver is enlarged and tender.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his new signs?
o: Right heart failure secondary to left heart failure
questions.e: Long-standing left-sided failure raises pulmonary pressures, which strains the right ventricle and precipitates right-sided failure (congestive cardiac failure).

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: legs have swollen to the thighs
JVP is raised to the earlobes
steps.x: Years of LVF, now raised JVP, hepatomegaly and oedema = the **right side has failed too**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Right heart failure secondary to left heart failure** (congestive cardiac failure).

elim: Possible but rare; long-standing LVF progressing to the right side is far more likely.
Would not raise the JVP; this liver is congested, not cirrhotic.
Causes leg oedema but the JVP would not be raised.
Causes oedema without a raised JVP.

steps.x: **E. Right heart failure secondary to left heart failure.** Long-standing failure of one side can precipitate failure of the other.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has 3 months of breathlessness walking to the shops and ankle swelling. She had a myocardial infarction 3 years ago. Her NT-proBNP is 2400 ng/L (under 400). Transthoracic echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with globally poor contraction and an ejection fraction of 30%.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate classification of her heart failure?
o: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
questions.e: An EF of 30% with a dilated, poorly contracting LV is HFrEF from impaired systolic contractility; HFpEF needs an EF above 50%.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
EF 30% with poor contraction = **systolic** failure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Heart failure is classed by EF: this is **HFrEF**.

elim: That needs an EF above 50%; hers is 30%.
Has a normal echo and a preserved EF, usually from anaemia, pregnancy or hyperthyroidism.
Shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a normal or high EF.
The left ventricle is the one that is dilated and poorly contracting.

steps.x: **B. Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.** EF reduced = HFrEF; EF above 50% = HFpEF.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has 2 months of breathlessness and ankle swelling. She has very heavy periods. Her pulse rate is 116 bpm and bounding, BP 124/58 mmHg. She has a soft flow murmur and mild ankle oedema. Echocardiography shows normal structure with an ejection fraction of 66% and normal diastolic filling.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her heart failure?
questions.e: Severe anaemia causes high-output heart failure: the heart is structurally normal with a preserved EF and normal filling, which separates it from true structural HF.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Menorrhagia, bounding pulse and a **normal echo** with EF 66% = **high-output** failure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: High-output failure from blood loss: **severe anaemia**.

elim: Gives a dilated LV with a low EF; her echo is normal.
Shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy on echo.
Would show a narrowed mitral valve on echo.
She is not pregnant or recently delivered, and it gives a low EF.

steps.x: **E. Severe anaemia.** High-output HF (anaemia, pregnancy, hyperthyroidism): normal echo, EF above 55%.

questions.stem: An 81 year old woman with 20 years of poorly controlled hypertension has 4 months of exertional breathlessness and ankle swelling. Her BP is 172/94 mmHg and pulse rate 76 bpm. Her NT-proBNP is raised. She has no murmur.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on her transthoracic echocardiogram?
o: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with outflow obstruction
Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with ejection fraction 60%
Dilated left ventricle with ejection fraction 25%
Normal structure with high cardiac output
questions.e: Long-standing hypertension gives a thick, stiff ventricle that contracts normally but fills poorly: HFpEF with EF above 50%. HOCM has asymmetric septal hypertrophy instead.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Elderly hypertensive woman with HF and no murmur = classic **HFpEF** (diastolic dysfunction).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A thick, stiff ventricle with normal EF: **concentric LVH, EF 60%**.

elim: This is HOCM, usually in a younger patient with a murmur.
Typical of HFrEF after MI; hypertension alone classically gives a stiff, thick ventricle.
That is high-output failure from anaemia, pregnancy or hyperthyroidism.
That is tamponade, which presents acutely.

steps.x: **B. Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with ejection fraction 60%.** HFpEF = EF above 50% with impaired relaxation; asymmetric septal hypertrophy = HOCM.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with ischaemic heart failure comes to clinic. He says he now uses three pillows. His apex beat is displaced to the anterior axillary line and he has fine bibasal crackles. His pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
questions.q: Which additional symptom is he most likely to describe?
o: Pleuritic chest pain on deep breathing
Productive cough of green sputum each winter
Waking at night gasping for breath
questions.e: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (waking gasping for breath) goes with orthopnoea in heart failure, as fluid redistributes to the lungs when lying flat.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Orthopnoea, displaced apex and crackles = **heart failure** with pulmonary congestion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The partner of orthopnoea: **paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea**.

elim: Suggests lung cancer or TB.
Suggests polycythaemia vera.
Suggests pleurisy or pulmonary embolism.
Suggests COPD or bronchiectasis.

steps.x: **E. Waking at night gasping for breath.** HF symptoms: breathlessness, orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling, weight gain.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman with known heart failure has gained 3 kg in 5 days. Her ankles and thighs are more swollen and she is more breathless. She ran out of her furosemide a week ago. Her pulse rate is 94 bpm, BP 142/84 mmHg and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. She has crackles to both mid-zones.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her weight gain?
o: Fluid retention from decompensated heart failure
questions.e: Rapid weight gain is fluid. Without her diuretic, RAAS-driven salt and water retention in heart failure has caused oedema and pulmonary congestion.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Weight up 3 kg in days, off diuretic, more oedema = **fluid overload**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Rapid weight gain here is fluid, from decompensated HF.

elim: Gains weight over months with central fat, not oedema over days.
Causes gradual weight gain, not 3 kg of oedema in 5 days.
Fat cannot be gained at 3 kg in 5 days.
Would cause oedema but not pulmonary crackles; stopping furosemide explains it.

steps.x: **B. Fluid retention from decompensated heart failure.** Rapid weight gain in HF = fluid; daily weights track it.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man had an anterior myocardial infarction 2 days ago. He suddenly becomes very breathless and is coughing pink frothy sputum. His pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 146/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 84% breathing air. He is cyanosed with crackles to the mid-zones. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral perihilar 'bat wing' shadowing with an enlarged heart: pulmonary oedema.

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his breathlessness?
questions.e: After an MI, a failing LV raises pulmonary venous pressure and floods the alveoli: pink frothy sputum, crackles, cyanosis and bilateral perihilar oedema.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Recent MI + pink frothy sputum + crackles + bilateral perihilar shadowing = **acute LVF**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fluid in the alveoli from the failing heart: **cardiogenic pulmonary oedema**.

elim: Needs a trigger such as sepsis or trauma, and the heart is normal size.
He has no fever, and pink frothy sputum points to oedema.
Gives a clear chest X-ray and no frothy sputum or crackles.
Gives absent breath sounds on one side, tracheal deviation and hypotension.

steps.x: **C. Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.** Pink frothy sputum after MI = acute left ventricular failure with pulmonary oedema.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with HFrEF had spironolactone added to ramipril and bisoprolol 3 weeks ago. He now feels weak and has palpitations. His pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg. He has not been unwell and is eating and drinking normally. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of these results?
questions.e: Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) cause hyperkalaemia and AKI, especially combined with an ACE inhibitor. Loop diuretics cause hypokalaemia.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
A new aldosterone antagonist on top of an ACE inhibitor, then high potassium and rising creatinine.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Potassium-sparing aldosterone antagonist: **spironolactone**.

elim: Causes bradycardia but not a rise in potassium and creatinine of this size on its own.
Would not explain a potassium of 6.4 starting soon after a new drug.
Loop diuretics lower potassium.
Can impair renal function, but the timing points to the new potassium-sparing drug.

steps.x: **D. Spironolactone.** MRA side effects: hyperkalaemia, AKI, gynaecomastia (spironolactone).

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has HFrEF with an ejection fraction of 32%. She does not have diabetes. A new drug was added to her ramipril, bisoprolol and eplerenone 2 months ago. She now has her second urinary tract infection in 6 weeks, with dysuria and frequency. Her BP is 116/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which new drug is most likely to have caused this?
questions.e: SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) are the fourth of the big 4 in HFrEF, even without diabetes; glucose in the urine raises the risk of UTI and genital thrush.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
She is on three of the big 4; the fourth is an SGLT2 inhibitor, which makes the urine sugary.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: SGLT2 inhibitor causing recurrent UTIs: **dapagliflozin**.

elim: Causes thyroid, lung and liver toxicity, not UTIs.
Causes nausea, visual change and arrhythmias.
Causes frequency from diuresis but not infections.
Causes bradycardia and visual flashes (phosphenes).

steps.x: **B. Dapagliflozin.** HFrEF big 4: ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor. SGLT2i side effect: UTI.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man sees his GP with 2 months of breathlessness and mild ankle swelling. He has hypertension. His pulse rate is 80 bpm, BP 144/86 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. His chest is clear and JVP not raised.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate interpretation of this result?
o: Arrange a transthoracic echocardiogram within 2 weeks
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction is likely
questions.e: BNP rises with ventricular wall strain, so it has a high negative predictive value: a normal level makes heart failure highly unlikely and other causes should be sought.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.
A first-line BNP that is **normal**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Low BNP, high negative predictive value: **heart failure is highly unlikely**.

elim: Echo is done once BNP is raised; a normal BNP does not need it.
BNP can only raise suspicion; echo confirms. And this result is normal.
A normal BNP makes all types of heart failure unlikely.
There is no need; BNP is not a time-dependent marker like troponin.

steps.x: **C. Heart failure is highly unlikely.** BNP is the first-line rule-out test: low BNP = HF very unlikely.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has 3 months of breathlessness on exertion, orthopnoea and ankle swelling. She had a myocardial infarction 4 years ago. Her pulse rate is 86 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. She has bibasal crackles. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Once BNP is raised, a transthoracic echocardiogram is the gold-standard test to confirm heart failure, measure EF and look for structural causes.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.
Classic HF picture with a **very high BNP**. BNP raises suspicion; it does not confirm.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: BNP up, so confirm with a **transthoracic echocardiogram**.

elim: Useful for specific cardiomyopathies, but not the first confirmatory test.
Looks for the cause but does not confirm heart failure.
Looks for PE; nothing here suggests it.
Detects myocardial injury, not heart failure.

steps.x: **E. Transthoracic echocardiogram.** BNP first; if raised, transthoracic echo confirms (gold standard).

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has confirmed heart failure. His GP wants to know which drug regimen to start. He is breathless on moderate exertion and has mild ankle oedema. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg. He has had his transthoracic echocardiogram.
questions.q: Which echocardiogram measurement most directly decides his choice of drug treatment?
questions.e: Echo measures the ejection fraction, which classifies HFrEF or HFpEF; HFrEF gets the big 4 and HFpEF gets an SGLT2 inhibitor first-line.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.
Treatment depends on whether this is HFrEF or HFpEF.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The number that sorts HFrEF from HFpEF: **ejection fraction**.

elim: Matters in Marfan syndrome or aortic disease, not HF drug choice.
Estimates right atrial pressure; does not decide the regimen.
Predicts AF but does not decide the regimen.
Relevant to constrictive pericarditis.

steps.x: **B. Ejection fraction.** Echo assesses EF and structure; EF decides HFrEF (big 4) vs HFpEF (SGLT2i).

questions.stem: An 84 year old woman with known heart failure is admitted with 1 week of worsening breathlessness and orthopnoea. Her pulse rate is 100 bpm, BP 150/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. She has crackles at both bases and dullness at both bases. Her chest X-ray shows an enlarged heart and Kerley B lines.
questions.q: Which additional finding is most likely on her chest X-ray?
questions.e: Raised pulmonary venous pressure diverts blood to the upper lobes. With cardiomegaly and Kerley B lines, heart failure also gives bilateral effusions (dull bases) and fluid in the horizontal fissure.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.

clues: enlarged heart and Kerley B lines
steps.x: Cardiomegaly + Kerley B lines = heart failure on CXR (ABCDE: alveolar oedema, B lines, cardiomegaly, diversion, effusions).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The 'D' of the heart failure X-ray: **upper lobe blood diversion**.

elim: Suggests sarcoidosis.
Suggests COPD.
Suggests TB or a cavitating cancer.
Suggests a perforated viscus.

steps.x: **E. Upper lobe blood diversion.** HF chest X-ray: alveolar oedema (bat wing), Kerley B lines, cardiomegaly, upper lobe diversion, effusions.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department at 3 am with sudden severe breathlessness. He is sweaty and coughing pink frothy sputum. His pulse rate is 122 bpm, BP 164/96 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 82% breathing air. There are crackles throughout both lungs.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his chest X-ray?
o: Lobar consolidation with an air bronchogram
Reticular shadowing at both bases with small lungs
questions.e: Acute LVF floods the alveoli around the hila first, giving the bilateral perihilar 'bat wing' pattern of alveolar oedema.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.
Sudden breathlessness with pink frothy sputum and widespread crackles = **acute pulmonary oedema**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Alveolar oedema on CXR: **'bat wing' perihilar shadowing**.

elim: Suggests pneumonia; he has no fever.
Suggests pulmonary fibrosis, a chronic process.
Suggests a pneumothorax.
A rare sign of pulmonary infarction from PE.

steps.x: **A. Bilateral perihilar 'bat wing' shadowing.** Bat wing shadowing = alveolar oedema = acute left ventricular failure.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman with stable heart failure is admitted with 3 days of worsening breathlessness and palpitations. Her pulse rate is 138 bpm and irregularly irregular, BP 122/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. She has bibasal crackles. Her doctor wants to identify what precipitated the decompensation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: ECG and bloods are part of every HF work-up; an irregularly irregular pulse at 138 bpm needs a 12-lead ECG to confirm fast AF, a common trigger for decompensation.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.
Decompensated HF with an irregularly irregular fast pulse: likely **AF** as the precipitant.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Confirm the rhythm now: **12-lead ECG**.

elim: Not a first-line or emergency test.
Invasive; not first-line for finding a precipitant.
Records over 24 hours; this rhythm is present now.
Assesses airways disease, not a cardiac precipitant.

steps.x: **A. 12-lead ECG.** ECG and bloods are routine in HF; fast AF reduces filling and output and tips HF over.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with HFrEF is reviewed in heart failure clinic. He is comfortable at rest. He gets breathless and tired climbing two flights of stairs or walking briskly to the bus, which he could do easily a year ago. He has no ankle swelling. His BP is 122/74 mmHg.

visual.title: NYHA functional class
visual.label: Where is he?
visual.caption: NYHA class grades limitation of physical activity by heart failure symptoms.

questions.q: Which is the most likely New York Heart Association (NYHA) class?
questions.e: NYHA class II is slight limitation: comfortable at rest but breathless or tired with ordinary activity such as stairs.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.
Comfortable at rest, symptoms only with **ordinary** activity = slight limitation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Slight limitation of ordinary activity: **NYHA class II**.

elim: Class I has no limitation of ordinary activity.
Class III is breathless on minimal activity, such as walking around the house.
Class IV has symptoms at rest.
There are only four NYHA classes.

steps.x: **B. Class II.** NYHA I none, II ordinary activity, III minimal activity, IV at rest.

questions.stem: An 80 year old woman with ischaemic heart failure is seen at home by her GP. She is comfortable sitting in her chair, but becomes breathless walking from the lounge to the kitchen or getting dressed. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely NYHA class?
questions.e: NYHA class III is marked limitation: comfortable at rest, but less than ordinary (minimal) activity like dressing causes symptoms.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.

clues: walking from the lounge to the kitchen
steps.x: Fine at rest; breathless with **minimal** activity.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Marked limitation, comfortable at rest: **NYHA class III**.

elim: No limitation; she is clearly limited.
Slight limitation only on ordinary activity such as stairs.
Symptoms at rest; she is comfortable sitting.
NYHA is a purely symptom-based (functional) class.

steps.x: **C. Class III.** NYHA III = comfortable at rest, symptomatic on minimal activity.
